commands.summary: Explain, request, approve and review access
commands.description:
Find out why someone has access, and grant temporary access instead of
permanent roles: request it for an hour, get it approved, and it expires
on its own.

commands.summary: Approve an access request
commands.description: Approve a request. The last required approval creates the time-limited grant. You can't approve your own request.

commands.summary: Immediately grant break-glass access and lift an active freeze
commands.description:
For incidents: immediately grant yourself Admin access for a short
window, lift any active freeze, and write a loud audit event. Needs the
`settings:manage` permission.

examples.run: clavis access break-glass --env prod --reason "SEV-1 checkout outage" --duration 1h

commands.summary: Explain why a user or group has access
commands.description: Explain why a member or group does or does not have a permission, step by step through roles and groups.

examples.run: clavis access explain ada@example.com --permission secrets:write --env prod
clavis access explain platform-team --permission secrets:read-values --project web-app

flags.name: user
flags.usage: member email, name, or user ID

commands.summary: Reject an access request
commands.description: Reject a request.

commands.summary: Request temporary project/environment access
commands.description: Ask for temporary access to an environment. Approvers get an email and, if configured, Slack, Teams or Discord buttons.

examples.run:
clavis access request --env prod --role Developer --duration 1h \
  --reason "Debugging checkout latency"

commands.description: List access requests. Members see their own; admins see everyone's.

commands.description: List every member and group that can read values in an environment, for periodic access reviews.

examples.run: clavis access review --env prod --format csv > access-review.csv

commands.summary: Instance administration
commands.description:
Maintenance commands that work on the database and keys directly. Run
them on the server (`docker exec clavis clavis admin ...`). Commands
that change keys or restore data need the server to be stopped.

examples.run: docker exec clavis clavis admin reset-password you@example.com
docker exec clavis clavis admin backup --out /data/backup.enc

commands.summary: Audit log administration
commands.description: Verify and sign the audit log's hash chain.

commands.summary: Sign the current audit chain head
commands.description: Sign the current head of the audit chain with the instance's Ed25519 key.

commands.summary: Verify the audit hash chain and signed checkpoints
commands.description: Recompute the audit hash chain and check signed checkpoints. Any edited or deleted event breaks the chain.

commands.summary: Create an encrypted consistent database backup
commands.description:
Write an encrypted, consistent snapshot of the database (SQLite
`VACUUM INTO` or `pg_dump`). The backup contains wrapped organization
keys, so keep the root key separately: without it the backup can't be
read.

examples.title: Docker
examples.run:
docker exec clavis clavis admin backup --out /data/backup.enc
docker cp clavis:/data/backup.enc ./

commands.summary: Copy a SQLite database into Postgres
commands.description: Copy a SQLite database into Postgres. The target is migrated and must be empty unless you pass `--force`.

commands.summary: Print a one-time password reset link for a user (no email needed)
commands.description:
Print a one-time link that sets a new password for a user. Use it when
someone, including the only owner, is locked out and the server has no
email (SMTP) configured. The link is valid for 24 hours by default and
the reset is recorded in the audit log.

examples.title: Docker
examples.run: docker exec clavis clavis admin reset-password you@example.com

commands.notes: Anyone with the link can set the password, so send it over a channel you trust.

flags.name: valid-for
flags.usage: how long the link stays valid (max 168h)

commands.summary: Restore an encrypted database backup
commands.description: Restore an encrypted backup while the server is stopped. The previous SQLite database is kept with a timestamp suffix.

commands.summary: Initialise or rotate the instance root key while the server is stopped
commands.description:
Create (`--init`) or rotate the root key while the server is stopped.
Every organization key and TOTP secret is re-encrypted, and the old key
is backed up.

flags.name: config
flags.usage: configuration file (default: CLAVIS_CONFIG or data defaults)

flags.name: init
flags.usage: create the root key if it does not exist

commands.summary: Split the root key into Shamir shares
commands.description: Split the root key into shares so that several people must come together to start the server.

commands.summary: Split the root key into threshold shares
commands.description: Split the root key into `--shares` pieces, any `--threshold` of which rebuild it. `--seal` removes the root key, so the server won't start until unsealed.
commands.notes: Shares are as sensitive as the root key. Store them offline, with different people.

flags.name: seal
flags.usage: remove the root key file after writing shares

commands.summary: Show the server's HTTPS certificate and its fingerprint
commands.description:
Show the certificate the server presents: TLS mode, names, issuer,
expiry, and the SHA-256 fingerprints of the certificate and of its
public key. Share the fingerprint with your team so they can check it
when `clavis login` asks them to trust a self-signed server.

With `CLAVIS_ACME_DNS`, it also says whether the Let's Encrypt
certificate has been issued yet, or whether the temporary self-signed
one is still in use.

examples.title: Docker
examples.run: docker exec clavis clavis admin tls-info

commands.summary: Reconstruct the root key from Shamir shares
commands.description: Rebuild the root key from enough shares, verify it, and let the server start again.

examples.run: clavis admin unseal --share share-01.key --share share-03.key --share share-05.key

commands.notes: Needs `keys.provider=file`.

flags.name: force
flags.usage: overwrite an existing root key file

commands.summary: Manage AI agent identities and command allowlists
commands.description:
Agent identities let coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ...)
run approved commands with secrets, through [`clavis mcp`](./mcp),
without seeing the values. Allowlists are deny-all by default and live
on the server, so an agent can't edit its own.

commands.summary: Add command patterns to an agent allowlist
commands.description: Approve command patterns for an agent. Patterns support `*` and `?`; a bare `*` is refused.

examples.run: clavis agents allow coding-agent "go test ./..." "pnpm dev"

commands.summary: List agent identities
commands.description: List agent identities and whether their allowlist is still deny-all.

commands.summary: Remove command patterns from an agent allowlist
commands.description: Remove patterns, or `--clear` to go back to deny-all.

commands.summary: Read the organization audit log
commands.description: Every read, write, reveal, sign-in and admin action is recorded in a tamper-evident audit log. Values are never in it.

commands.summary: List recent audit events
commands.description: List recent audit events for the organization.

flags.name: after
flags.usage: only events after this sequence number

commands.summary: Validate an environment against the project's secret schema
commands.notes: Exits with code `6` when a check fails, so `clavis check --env production` can gate a deploy in CI.

flags.name: all
flags.usage: check every environment in the project

commands.summary: Generate typed config loaders from the project schema
commands.description:
Generate a typed config loader from the project [schema](./schema), so
your app fails at startup with a clear message when a key is missing or
malformed.
commands.notes:
- TypeScript exports a zod schema, the inferred type and `loadConfig`.
- Go exports a struct, `Load`, `LoadFor(envType)` and `LoadFrom(environ)`.
- Python exports a pydantic `Config` and `load_config`.

Loaders parse env-style strings: integers become numbers, booleans accept
`true/false/1/0/yes/no`, JSON fields are decoded, enums and patterns are
checked. Keys required in any environment type are required fields.

A connection stores one provider credential for the whole organization:

updates every sync that uses it. Credentials are never shown again.

examples.run: clavis connections create "Home Forgejo" --provider forgejo --url https://git.example.com --token -

commands.summary: Manage machine and workload identities
commands.description:
Identities are non-human users: CI pipelines, servers, Kubernetes
workloads and AI agents. They get a token, or exchange a workload OIDC
token (GitHub Actions, GitLab, Kubernetes, AWS, GCP) for a short-lived
one, so no long-lived secret sits in CI.

commands.summary: Create a machine or workload identity and its first token
commands.description: Create a machine identity and print its first token (shown once), or set up keyless OIDC trust.

examples.title: Token for a deploy server
examples.run: clavis identities create deploy-bot --role Developer --project web-app --identity-env prod

examples.title: GitHub Actions, no stored token
examples.run:
clavis identities create github-actions \
  --oidc github --repo acme/web --branch main --gh-environment production \
  --role Developer --project web-app --identity-env prod

examples.title: GitLab CI
examples.run:
clavis identities create gitlab-ci \
  --oidc gitlab --repo group/project --branch main --audience clavis

examples.title: Kubernetes service account
examples.run:
clavis identities create k8s-deployer \
  --oidc kubernetes --issuer https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local \
  --audience clavis --k8s-namespace apps --k8s-service-account deployer

examples.title: AWS IAM role
examples.run:
clavis identities create aws-ci --aws-account 123456789012 \
  --aws-arn 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-*' \
  --project web-app --identity-env dev

examples.title: Google Cloud service account
examples.run:
clavis identities create gcp-deployer \
  --oidc gcp --gcp-service-account deployer@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

examples.title: Any OIDC issuer
examples.run:
clavis identities create ci \
  --oidc generic --issuer https://idp.example.com --audience clavis \
  --claim ref=refs/heads/main

commands.notes: With OIDC, the pipeline exchanges its own token at `POST /api/v1/auth/oidc` (AWS: a signed STS `GetCallerIdentity` request at `/api/v1/auth/aws`) for a short-lived Clavis token.

commands.summary: Import secrets from files or external providers
commands.description:
Import `.env`, JSON or YAML files, or pull everything from another secret
manager. A folder is walked recursively and each file's directory becomes
the secret folder. Try `--dry-run` first: it shows what would be new,
changed or unchanged, never values.

examples.title: HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao (KV v1 or v2)
Google Secret Manager
examples.run:
clavis import --provider gcp --gcp-project my-project \
  --gcp-service-account service-account.json --gcp-prefix APP_ --dry-run

commands.notes:
A map file renames keys and folders; an empty target drops the key:

```yaml
keys:
  OLD_DATABASE_URL: DATABASE_URL
  DROP_ME: ""
folders:
  "": /imported
  legacy: /legacy
```

Provider credentials can also come from their usual environment
variables: `INFISICAL_TOKEN`, `DOPPLER_TOKEN`, `VAULT_ADDR`,
`VAULT_TOKEN`, `OPENBAO_ADDR`, `OPENBAO_TOKEN`, `OP_CONNECT_HOST`,
`OP_CONNECT_TOKEN`, `OP_VAULT`, `AWS_REGION`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`,
`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, `GCP_PROJECT` and
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`.

The web app's **Import** dialog accepts `.env` or JSON with the same
dry-run preview.

flags.name: aws-prefix
flags.usage: only import secrets with this name prefix

flags.name: dry-run
flags.usage: preview new, changed, and unchanged keys without writing

flags.name: gcp-prefix
flags.usage: only import secrets with this name prefix

flags.name: kind
flags.usage: secret, variable, or file (default: preserve provider kind, else secret)

flags.name: map
flags.usage: YAML/JSON key and folder mapping file

flags.name: provider
flags.usage: file, infisical, doppler, vault, onepassword, aws, or gcp

commands.summary: Link this directory to a project
commands.description:
Link the current folder to an organization, project and default
environment by writing [`.clavis.yaml`](./clavis-yaml). The file holds no
secrets, so commit it: everyone on the team then gets the same context.

`init` asks for anything it can't work out, offers to import an existing
`.env`, and detects how to start your app (`package.json` scripts,
`bin/rails`, `manage.py`, `artisan`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, Maven,
Gradle, Docker Compose) so a plain `clavis run` works right away.

flags.name: project-name
flags.usage: create a project with this name if none exist

commands.summary: Create and manage dynamic secret leases
commands.description:
Dynamic secrets: instead of one shared database password, issue a fresh
Postgres role or AWS STS credentials per use, which expire on their own.

commands.summary: Create a PostgreSQL or AWS STS dynamic secret config
commands.description: Describe how to issue credentials: a Postgres server and the role to grant, or an AWS role to assume.

examples.title: Postgres
examples.run:
clavis lease config-create --host db.internal --database app \
  --username clavis_admin --password "$PGPASSWORD" \
  --grant-role app_readwrite --default-ttl 3600 --max-ttl 86400

examples.title: AWS STS
examples.run:
clavis lease config-create --engine aws --aws-region eu-central-1 \
  --aws-access-key "$AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID" --aws-secret-key "$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" \
  --aws-role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy

commands.notes: AWS leases return `access_key_id`, `secret_access_key`, `session_token` and `expiration`. STS credentials can't be renewed; create a new lease.

commands.summary: Sign in with a browser (device code)
commands.description:
Sign in with your browser. Clavis shows a short code, opens the approval
page, and saves the token in the OS keychain (or in the file named by
`CLAVIS_CREDENTIAL_FILE`). The server is remembered, so later commands
don't need `--server`.

On a machine without a browser (SSH session, container), pass
`--no-browser` and open the printed link on any other device.

If the server uses a self-signed certificate (`CLAVIS_TLS=self-signed`,
common on a LAN), `login` shows the certificate's fingerprint and asks
whether to trust it. The answer is remembered for this server, so you
are asked once per computer. See [`clavis trust`](./trust).

examples.title: Sign in from an SSH session

commands.notes:
In CI and other automation, don't log in: set `CLAVIS_TOKEN` to a machine
token instead. See [environment variables](./environment-variables).

flags.name: no-browser
flags.usage: do not open the browser automatically

commands.summary: Sign out and delete the saved token
commands.description: Revoke the saved session on the server and delete the local credential.

commands.summary: Run a Model Context Protocol server over stdio
commands.description:
Run a Model Context Protocol server over stdio for Claude Code, Cursor,
Codex, Windsurf or any MCP client. It offers four tools:
`list_secrets` (names only), `check_env`, `run_with_secrets` (allowlisted
commands, masked output) and `request_secret` (asks a human).

With `--agent NAME`, it uses your own `clavis login` to start a one-hour
agent session held in memory, so the MCP config contains no token.

examples.title: Claude Code
examples.run: claude mcp add clavis -- clavis mcp --agent coding-agent

commands.notes:
Masking reduces accidental leaks but is not a security boundary: an
allowed command still receives the secrets, and if it runs code the
agent wrote, the agent could read them. Prefer short-lived credentials
([leases](./lease)) for agent workflows. A static agent token in
`CLAVIS_TOKEN` still works for headless agents.

flags.name: agent
flags.usage: agent identity name; starts an in-memory session with your login (env CLAVIS_AGENT)

commands.summary: Schedule and run secret rotation
commands.description:
Rotate secrets automatically: a Postgres role password, an AWS IAM
access key, or anything behind your own webhook. The **Rotation** page

clavis rotation create DATABASE_PASSWORD --provider postgres \
  --pg-host db.internal --pg-database app --pg-username admin \

commands.summary: Run a command with secrets injected and output masked
commands.description:
Start your app with the environment's secrets as environment variables.
Clavis starts the command itself, so you keep one terminal; anything the
command prints is masked, so secret values don't end up in logs.

Clavis flags go **before** the command. Everything from the first word of
the command on belongs to your command, so `--` is optional:
`clavis run rails s -p 3001` passes `-p 3001` to Rails.

Without a command, `clavis run` starts the `run:` command saved in
[`.clavis.yaml`](./clavis-yaml). `clavis init` fills it in when it
recognizes the project.

examples.title: File secrets become private temporary files
Use -- when your command itself starts with a dash

commands.notes:
- **Masking** replaces injected values in the command's output. It
  protects logs and screen shares; it is not a security boundary. Turn
  it off with `--no-mask` when you debug output.
- **`--watch`** listens for changes and restarts the command with fresh
  values whenever this environment's secrets change.
- **`--mount`** writes `file` secrets to a `0700` temporary directory as
  `0600` files, puts each file's path in the variable, and removes the
  directory when the command exits.
- **Offline:** with `cache: true` in `.clavis.yaml`, the last values are
  used for up to 24 hours when the server is unreachable. See
  [offline cache](./offline-cache).
- `clavis run` exits with your command's exit code.

flags.name: mount
flags.usage: write file secrets to a private temp directory and expose their paths as env vars

flags.name: watch
flags.usage: restart the command when the environment's secrets change

commands.summary: Scan files for leaked Clavis tokens and secret values
commands.description:
Look for leaked secrets in files: Clavis token formats, and (if you can
read values) the actual values of this environment's secrets, matched in
memory. Findings name the file, line and key, never the value.
commands.notes: Exits with code `7` when it finds a leak, so it can fail CI. `--values=false` checks token formats only.

commands.summary: Manage the project secret schema
commands.description:
A schema lists the keys a project needs, with a type, kind, pattern and
which environment types require them. Keep it in git as
`clavis.schema.yaml` and review changes like code. [`clavis check`](./check)
validates environments against it and [`clavis codegen`](./codegen) turns
it into a typed loader.
commands.notes:
```yaml
DATABASE_URL:
  type: url
  kind: secret
  required: { development: true, production: true }
  description: Primary Postgres connection string
LOG_LEVEL:
  type: enum
  kind: variable
  values: [debug, info, warn, error]
```

Types: `string`, `url`, `int`, `bool`, `json`, `enum`. Kinds: `secret`,
`variable`, `file`. Optional `pattern` (regular expression), `example`
and `description`.

commands.summary: Trust a server's self-signed certificate on this computer
commands.description:
Decide which self-signed server certificates this computer accepts.
Certificates from a public authority (Let's Encrypt, your company CA in
the system store) need nothing here.

The first time the CLI meets a self-signed server, it shows the
certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint and asks you to trust it, like SSH does
with a new host. The answer is pinned to the server's public key, so it
survives the yearly certificate renewal and a change of the server's
address. If the key ever changes, the CLI stops with a warning and asks
you to type `trust` to accept the new one.

Compare the fingerprint with the one the server prints
(`docker exec clavis clavis admin tls-info`) or with the one an admin
sent you.

examples.title: Trust without a prompt (scripts, onboarding docs)

commands.notes:
Other ways to trust a server, for automation:

- `CLAVIS_SERVER_FINGERPRINT`: the expected SHA-256 of the certificate or its public key. Nothing is saved.
- `CLAVIS_CA_CERT`: a PEM file (or a list of them) with your own CA, added to the system roots.
- `CLAVIS_TRUST_FILE`: where pins are stored, instead of `trusted-servers.json` in the config folder.

To avoid the question entirely, give the server a real certificate: with
a domain you control, set `CLAVIS_ACME_DNS` and the server gets one from
Let's Encrypt even on a private network.

commands.summary: Check a server's certificate and trust it
commands.description:
Connect to the server, show its certificate (subject, expiry, SHA-256
fingerprint) and ask whether to trust it. Without an argument it uses
the server from `--server` or `.clavis.yaml`.

With `--fingerprint`, nothing is asked: the certificate is trusted if it
matches, and refused otherwise. Both the certificate fingerprint and the
public key fingerprint are accepted, with or without colons.

If the certificate is already trusted (by the system or by an earlier
pin), `trust add` says so and changes nothing.
commands.notes: In a script without a terminal, `trust add` without `--fingerprint` fails and prints the fingerprint to check, instead of trusting blindly.

flags.name: fingerprint
flags.usage: expected SHA-256 of the certificate or its public key; trusts without asking

topics.title: .clavis.yaml
topics.summary: The per-folder file that links a repository to a project. Commit it; it holds no secrets.
topics.body:
`clavis init` writes `.clavis.yaml` in your repository. Commands look for
it in the current folder and its parents, so they work from any
subfolder without flags.

```yaml
server: https://clavis.example.com
org: acme
project: web-app
env: dev               # default environment
path: /                # default folder
run: bin/rails server  # what a plain `clavis run` starts
branch_envs: true      # use the git branch's preview environment
cache: true            # encrypted offline cache for `clavis run`
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `server` | Server URL. Saved by `clavis login`. |
| `org`, `project` | Organization and project slugs. |
| `env` | Default environment. `--env` overrides it per command. |
| `path` | Default folder inside the environment. |
| `run` | Command started by `clavis run` with no arguments. Quotes and backslashes work as in a shell; pipes and `&&` don't (put those in a script). |
| `branch_envs` | When `true`, use the preview environment of the current git branch if one exists. See [`clavis env branch`](./env-branch). |
| `cache` | When `true`, keep an encrypted copy of the last values for offline use. See [offline cache](./offline-cache). |

## Which value wins

For server, organization, project and environment, the first one set
wins:

1. the flag (`--env staging`)
2. the environment variable (`CLAVIS_ENV=staging`)
3. `.clavis.yaml`
4. the default (`dev` for the environment)

examples.title: Save a default command, then start it
examples.run:
echo 'run: npm run dev' >> .clavis.yaml
clavis run

topics.title: Environment variables
topics.summary: Variables the CLI reads, for CI, containers and scripts.
topics.body:
| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `CLAVIS_TOKEN` | Machine or agent token. Used instead of `clavis login`, for CI. |
| `CLAVIS_SERVER` | Server URL, like `--server`. |
| `CLAVIS_ORG`, `CLAVIS_PROJECT`, `CLAVIS_ENV` | Like `--org`, `--project`, `--env`. Override `.clavis.yaml`. |
| `CLAVIS_AGENT` | Agent identity for `clavis mcp`, like `--agent`. |
| `CLAVIS_CREDENTIAL_FILE` | Keep the login token in this file (mode `0600`) instead of the OS keychain. Useful in containers. |
| `CLAVIS_CACHE_DIR` | Where the offline cache lives. |
| `CLAVIS_SERVER_FINGERPRINT` | Expected SHA-256 of a self-signed server's certificate or public key. Trusts it without a prompt. |
| `CLAVIS_CA_CERT` | PEM file(s) with your own certificate authority, added to the system roots. Separate several with `:`. |
| `CLAVIS_TRUST_FILE` | Where trusted self-signed servers are stored. Default: `trusted-servers.json` in the config folder. |
| `NO_COLOR` | Turn off colors. They are also off when output isn't a terminal. |

Server settings (`CLAVIS_TLS`, `CLAVIS_SERVER_BASE_URL`,
`CLAVIS_SETUP_TOKEN`, ...) are described in the self-hosting guide.

examples.title: CI with a machine token
examples.run:
export CLAVIS_TOKEN=clv_mt_…
clavis run --project web-app --env production ./deploy.sh

topics.title: Exit codes
topics.summary: Stable exit codes, so scripts and CI can react to what went wrong.
topics.body:
| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Success |
| `1` | General error |
| `2` | Wrong usage: unknown flag, missing argument |
| `3` | Not signed in, or the token expired. Run `clavis login`. |
| `4` | Signed in, but not allowed to do this |
| `5` | Not found: organization, project, environment or key |
| `6` | Validation failed (`clavis check`) |
| `7` | Leak found (`clavis scan`) |

`clavis run` and `clavis lease run` exit with your command's own exit
code.

topics.title: Output and scripting
topics.summary: Readable tables in a terminal, JSON for scripts, and confirmations for production.
topics.body:
- In a terminal, commands print colored tables and ask before risky
  changes. When output is piped, colors turn off.
- `--json` prints machine-readable output on every command that returns
  data.
- Writes to a **production** environment show a red banner and ask you to
  type the project name. In scripts, pass `--yes`. An organization can
  block CLI writes to production entirely.
- Every error says how to fix it, for example `Not logged in. Run: clavis login`.

topics.title: Offline cache
topics.summary: Keep working when the server is unreachable.
topics.body:
With `cache: true` in `.clavis.yaml` (`clavis init` sets it),
`clavis run` saves an AES-256-GCM encrypted copy of the values after each
successful fetch. If the server can't be reached, it uses that copy for
up to 24 hours and prints a warning.

The cache key is kept in the OS keychain (or the credential file), and
each cache is tied to one server, organization, project and environment.
Set `cache: false` to turn it off for a project. Delete the cache folder
(or `CLAVIS_CACHE_DIR`) to clear it.

topics.title: Overlays
topics.summary: Per-tenant or per-region values on top of an environment.
topics.body:
An overlay overrides selected keys without changing the environment
itself, for example different endpoints per region. Pass `--overlay` to
`run`, `export`, `secrets ls` or `secrets get`. Overlays are created in
the web app and appear as extra columns in the secrets grid.

topics.title: Shell completion
topics.summary: Tab completion for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell.
topics.body: `clavis completion <shell>` prints a completion script for your shell.
